Nick

> Hi Nick,
> I tried adding "stratified=FALSE" (my analysis wasn't time-stratified) but still crashed...

> > check_ML_vs_BSM(res, clado_events_tables, model_name, tr=NULL, plot_each_node=FALSE, linreg_plot=TRUE, MultinomialCI=TRUE,stratified=FALSE)

>
> Error in check_ML_vs_BSM(res, clado_events_tables, model_name, tr = NULL,  :

>   参数没有用(stratified = FALSE)
> It said the parameter "stratified = FALSE" was useless. What's wrong?

I meant do it like this:

================
library(MultinomialCI)
stratified = FALSE

check_ML_vs_BSM(res, clado_events_tables, model_name, tr=NULL, plot_each_node=FALSE, linreg_plot=TRUE, MultinomialCI=TRUE)

================

Probably, "stratified = FALSE" was somewhere else in the original script, and it got deleted or skipped or something.  If that doesn't work, edit the "check_ML_vs_BSM" source code and put stratified = FALSE in there.  But this function has worked for everyone else so I think the above will work.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: tip ranges same order as tree?
messages.subject_clean: tip ranges same order as tree?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a quick question. Must the species in the tip ranges object be in the same order as listed in the phylogeny for everything to work correctly? I am running a DEC model in BioGeoBEARS. I know the function "order_tipranges_by_tree_tips" exists for this purpose, but it's not clear to me if this is a requirement or not (I have already started running my analysis).

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Sep 4, 2017 at 2:29 AM, <lizmil...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I have a quick question. Must the species in the tip ranges object be in the same order as listed in the phylogeny for everything to work correctly? I am running a DEC model in BioGeoBEARS. I know the function "order_tipranges_by_tree_tips" exists for this purpose, but it's not clear to me if this is a requirement or not (I have already started running my analysis).

Hi -- no, this is not a requirement.  I don't remember exactly, but probably I use "order_tipranges_by_tree_tips" internally to get the geog-file data into the right order for the storage of the downpass likelihoods.

So, don't worry about this.  The areas should be in the same order in the geog file, and in the distances matrix, the connectivity matrix, etc., if you use those.  There is an error check that should give an error message if they don't line up, though.

Cheers!
nick

On Tue, Sep 12, 2017 at 2:01 AM, 张睿 <xiaor...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Sorry, I have got two more questions:
>
> How could I rotate a branch of phylogenetic tree?

The APE function for this is "rotate", I think.

> And is there a function similar with “oder nodes decreasing / increasing” in FigTree?

I think the APE function is ladderize().

> Thanks!

However, you cannot rotate nodes, stick that tree into an already-done BioGeoBEARS analysis, and then expect the plotting to come out OK.  This is because the state/range probabilities are stored in a specific order, and the order will change if you change the tree.

It wouldn't be mind-bogglingly difficult to write some code to re-order the stored state/range probabilities to match some reordered tree -- you could do it with the BioGeoBEARS prt() function, which prints the tree to a table.  Make sure to set get_tipnames=TRUE to get the alphabetical list of the species names in each clade on the tree, this is a unique list that can be matched between the new tree and old tree with the match() function.

Easiest option: alter your tree in FigTree so it looks like you want, save that to Newick, use the new Newick file for re-running the BioGeoBEARS analysis with the new tree.

Note: I think FigTree displays trees "flipped" vertically, compared to how the identical Newick file will display in R.

Harder option: alter your tree in FigTree or R so it looks like you want, save that to Newick, use prt() and match() to re-order all of the probabilities tables in the saved BioGeoBEARS objects to match the new tree, give the BioGeoBEARS objects the new Newick file, then plot the old BioGeoBEARS results on the new tree.

Cheers,
Nick

PS: The links below will help -- but it will take some serious study of them:

Table of probabilities of states/ranges at each node
http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#node_probabilities

Fwd: state/range probabilities at each node in BioGeoBEARS...and other google group posts...
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/biogeobears/eGzLRPg10y0

And see especially:

Some code for working with phylo objects in R http://luisdva.github.io/edge-lengths/  cc @jeff_o_hanson @NickJMatzke
https://twitter.com/LuisDVerde/status/836361904645943297

And this post on the use of prt():

(pasting the whole thing below for future Google-ability)

Making sense of trees
http://luisdva.github.io/rstats/edge-lengths/
==========================================
Making sense of trees

In the words of Nick Matzke:

R’s tree structure is pretty non-intuitive, compared to the “a tree is a collection of node objects” structure that is taught in most phylogenetics courses and used in e.g. C++ software. It’s done this way because R likes lists, and doesn’t like objects.

The structure of phylogenetic trees in R (namely APE’s phylo objects) can be confusing because much of the information needed to describe how different nodes and branches make up a tree is implicit.

I learned this the hard way during the early days of my PhD research. My thesis work revolved around phylogenetic lineage ages, so one of my very first tasks after finding a suitable tree was to get a table with species and their ‘edge lengths’ as a way to (more or less) represent their evolutionary ages. At this time I was very new to R and I lost months trying to figure this out on my own. After going over the APE book I slowly realized that lineage age information is contained within the phylo objects and that it can be extracted, but only if you ask nicely.

Phylo objects have a vector of edge lengths for every node, but I was unable to figure out how to get a list of tips and internal nodes that would match up with the vector of edge lengths. After much struggle, I figured out that the branching.times() function computes the distance from each node to the tips, producing a named vector that corresponds to the nodes in the tree. I also learned that the mrca() function produces a matrix of node numbers corresponding to the most recent common ancestors between pairs of tips or nodes. The next challenge would be to put the two together.

I’m writing this brief post because I found an R script from early 2012 in a random USB stick, in which coding superstar Jeff Hanson walked me through indexing, building loops, and functions in order to extract the species lineage ages for any phylogeny object.

The function below has a couple of loops that iterate through the mrca matrix and the branching times vector to produce a data frame of edge lengths for all the tree tips. The for loops make for slow processing if we have large trees but I was patient and that exact function created the main dataset that I analysed for a large part of my thesis. If you’re interested have a look at Jeff’s crisp programming to see how clever he was when coming up with the loops.

# extracting edge lengths from a phylo object
# define function
# note that the function requires ape to be installed

phylLages <- function(inputTree){
require(ape)
# numeric vector with the branching times for each tip
apedates<-branching.times(inputTree)
# matrix of tips and most recent common ancestors
mrca.matrix<-mrca(inputTree)

### preliminary procesing
Species = c()
Node_date = c()

### main processing
col_counter = 0

for (i in colnames(mrca.matrix)) {

  # keep track of which column we're in
  col_counter = col_counter + 1

  # print messege
  cat(paste("Starting species ", as.character(col_counter), " out of ", as.character(length(colnames(mrca.matrix))), "\n", sep=""))

  # add species name to export vector
  Species = append(Species, i)

  # extract a vector of node numbers for the species we're up to
  currNodeVec = mrca.matrix[,col_counter]
  # working out what the node dates are for each node for the species we're working with
  currNodeDates = c()
  row_counter = 0
  for (currNodeNum in currNodeVec) {
    row_counter = row_counter + 1
    if (row_counter != col_counter) {
      currNodeDates = append(currNodeDates, apedates[as.character(currNodeNum)])
    }
  }
  # find out what the minimum number is
  minDate = min(currNodeDates)
  Node_date = append(Node_date, minDate)

        }
  exportFrame = data.frame(Species,Node_date)
  cat("DONE!\n")
  return(exportFrame)
}
A few years later I learned that the BioGeoBEARS R package includes the prt() function, which Nick Matzke wrote specifically to print the content of a tree into a tabular format, making all the implicit information explicit. This function is faster and provides much more information, and I was very relieved to see that the edge lengths it provides are the same Jeff and I obtained with the custom function.

Lets have a look. Both functions keep the tip order so comparing the results is easy. This examples uses the built in tree of bird families (Sibley and Ahlquist 1990) from the ape package.

plotted with ggtree
# comparing the edge lengths with BioGeoBEARS::prt

# load libraries
library(ape)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(BioGeoBEARS)

# phylogeny of bird families (comes with ape)
data("bird.families")

# get a data frame of edge lengths using the Jeff Hanson & Luis Verde function
jhEdges <- phylLages(bird.families)

# get a data frame of edge lengths using prt
birdPrintout <- prt(bird.families)
## extract the data for the tips only
# note: the tips in this particular tree are families not species
birdPrintout_Tips <- birdPrintout %>% filter(str_detect(label,"Node")==FALSE) %>%
                        select(Species=label,Node_date=edge.length)
# quick comparison
head(jhEdges) == head(birdPrintout_Tips)

Now we can do side-by-side glimpse of the two data frames, and time how long the two functions take to process the data.

> bind_cols(jhEdges,birdPrintout_Tips) %>% head
        Species Node_date       Species Node_date
1 Struthionidae      17.1 Struthionidae      17.1
2       Rheidae      17.1       Rheidae      17.1
3   Casuariidae       9.5   Casuariidae       9.5
4   Apterygidae       9.5   Apterygidae       9.5
5     Tinamidae      21.8     Tinamidae      21.8
6      Cracidae      19.8      Cracidae      19.8
system.time(phylLages(bird.families))
system.time(prt(bird.families))
prt is about 4.5x faster than the loops, and this becomes relevant as the number of tips increases or in the case of multiphylo objects with varying edge lengths so I recommend using it for any work on edge lengths.
==========================================

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] How to add dispersal, "jump" dispersal and vicariance events to the figure?
messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] How to add dispersal, "jump" dispersal and vicariance events to the figure?
messages.body_plain:
Hi --

Briefly, there is no such thing as "plotting the events", straight from the ML results.  The ML results average over many possible event histories (thousands or millions of histories are possible, or really an infinite number, if you have any anagenetic events).

Options:

1. The most common thing people do is look at the ML results of the most-probable states, and mistakenly assume this is "the" history. I discourage this, except when the probabilities are very unambiguous:

The plot of most-probable states is not the same thing as the best joint history
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_joint

The plot of most-probable states is not the same thing as an estimate of event counts
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_events

2. The next most common thing is to look at the pie charts, and make a rational judgement about where a particular event (vicariance or whatever) seems highly plausible.  This is imperfect, but not too bad.

3. More sophisticated is to use Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping. This gives a sample of exact histories -- but then you have to decide which one to show, or show several, or whatever.   Even here, the events won't be labeled, you just have to look at the colors and figure out what happened.

You can use BSM to get percentage probabilities of each kind of event for each node or branch of the tree, but then displaying these on the tree would be its own problem.  This requires some strong abilities with working in R with data.frames, and understanding the APE tree structure and the prt() function.

(BSM too is imperfect -- it shares the assumptions of all DEC-style analyses, ie no extinction etc. See PhyloWiki)

Whichever of 1-3 is done, actually plotting labels like "vicariance event" would be a manual thing that you add after the analysis, using e.g. Powerpoint, Illustrator, Inkscape, etc.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Re: Automatically identifying nodes where specific evens occur
messages.body_plain:
Hi!  For your goals, BSM would be the best option. This will give you a big sample of event histories, and you could query any branch/node of interest and can what the sample of event histories was for that branch/node, and a sample of their timings.

For a sample of different trees, you would have to set up a big loop in R, and either

(a) run ML on each tree and then BSM on each tree,

(b) or you could decide to run ML on one tree (maybe the MCC tree) and then take those model parameters and use them for BSM on each tree.

Option (a) would be somewhat more correct, but probably would make little difference, if the data have strong support for a particular model, and if the tree is reasonably certain.

Option (b) would more fully account for those uncertainties, but would be slower.

Any of these options will require decent skill with for-loops in R, the APE tree structure and prt(), and working with the BSM event tables.

Yet another option is to do the phylogeny and biogeography jointly in RevBayes, there are tutorials on this, but I'm not sure if you can record event histories, and I'm not sure for how big of a problem the runtime is reasonable.

One other note below:

On Wed, Sep 20, 2017 at 8:33 PM, James Kitson <jamesk...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> So it seems I've misunderstood how the states are encoded in the results object. I had thought that the matrices variously labelled *AT_node* and *below_node* were encoding the state probabilities before and after estimated events (i.e. nodes vs corners)

AT_node is the probabilies (or likelihoods or whatever) at the node, which is at a branch top. This point is instantaneously before speciation.  Let's call it node X.

below_node is the probabilities (or likelihoods or whatever) at the BRANCH BOTTOM below that same node X.  This is the same as the corner below node X.  This point is instantaneously after the speciation of node Y, where node Y is the direct ancestor of node X.

All of this is somewhat confusing, but it's all a product of the APE tree structure, where each branch is attached to the node at the top of that branch.  You can use the prt() table to find out which nodes are above or below which other nodes.

> but these always have the same most probable state for all nodes so that can't be what's happening.

This shouldn't be true, except for the BAYAREALIKE model or other simple situations (everything living in area A or something).  Probably you are confusing which nodes and corners descend from each other.

> Instead, I think I need to compare most probable states for each daughter node with each parent node (i.e. what is the most probable state at nodes 10 and 9 and are they states of interest? Does this make sense or am I making this too complicated?
